events.title: Ashdod's revolt and a king sent back in chains
events.text: Ashdod rose against Sargon II and looked to Egypt for help. Sargon took the city, and its king Yamani fled to the land of Kush. A rock inscription of Sargon at Tang-i Var in Iran, published in 1999, tells the end: Shebitku, king of Kush, put Yamani in fetters and sent him to Assyria.
events.why: It showed every small king in the region what trusting Egypt was worth. The Bible gives the same years a prophet's sign: Isaiah walking barefoot for three years, so that whoever relied on Egypt and Kush would be put to shame.
claims: Ashdod's revolt and Sargon's capture of the city.
Shebitku of Kush extradites Yamani to Sargon.
Isaiah's sign against Egypt and Kush, the only place in the Bible that names Sargon: Isaiah 20.

events.title: Hezekiah's reform
events.text: The Book of Kings praises Hezekiah above all the kings of Judah. He removed the high places, smashed the sacred pillars, and broke the bronze serpent called Nehushtan, to which the people burned incense. Chronicles adds a great Passover in Jerusalem, to which he invited the north as well.
events.why: At Beersheba the stones of a large horned altar were found taken apart and reused in a storehouse wall, and at Arad a small shrine went out of use around the same time. Ze'ev Herzog links both with Hezekiah. Nadav Na'aman doubts that a reform as broad as the one in Kings took place.
claims: The reform, the high places and Nehushtan: 2 Kings 18:3–6.
The dismantled horned altar of Beersheba.
Arad and Beersheba as evidence of a reform.
The historicity of the reform doubted.

events.title: A king's seal: Hezekiah son of Ahaz
events.text: In a refuse heap on the Ophel, below the Temple Mount, Eilat Mazar's team found a clay seal impression about one centimetre across. It reads 'Belonging to Hezekiah [son of] Ahaz, king of Judah', beside a two-winged sun flanked by signs of life. On its back are the marks of the papyrus it once sealed.
events.why: It is the first impression of a seal of a king of Israel or Judah found in a scientific excavation. The Egyptian-style winged sun shows a royal emblem shared across the region.
claims: Text, emblem and find-spot of the bulla.

events.title: The Siloam tunnel
events.text: A tunnel about 533 metres long winds through the rock under the City of David, from the Gihon spring to the Pool of Siloam. In 1880 an inscription was found cut into its wall near the exit: the diggers 'struck each man towards his fellow, axe against axe, and the water flowed from the spring to the pool'.
events.why: The Bible says Hezekiah 'made the pool and the conduit and brought water into the city', and stopped the springs outside so that Assyria would find no water. Radiometric dates from the plaster point to about 700 BC; Ronny Reich and Eli Shukron argue the work began earlier.
claims: The tunnel and its inscription; now in the Istanbul Archaeology Museums.
Radiocarbon and uranium-thorium dates of about 700 BC.
An earlier start, late 9th or early 8th century BC.
Hezekiah's conduit and the stopped springs: 2 Kings 20:20; 2 Chronicles 32:3–4, 30.

events.title: The Broad Wall and the royal jars
events.text: In the Jewish Quarter, Nahman Avigad found a city wall about seven metres thick, built straight over houses that had been knocked down. All over Judah, handles of large storage jars carry a royal stamp, 'lmlk', 'belonging to the king', with one of four names: Hebron, Ziph, Socoh or MMST.
events.why: Both are often read as Hezekiah's preparations for war. Avigad compared the wall with Isaiah's words, 'you broke down the houses to fortify the wall'. Oded Lipschits and colleagues think the royal jar system began earlier, when Judah first became Assyria's vassal.
claims: The Broad Wall, about 7 m thick, over demolished houses.
'You broke down the houses to fortify the wall' (Isaiah 22:10).
The lmlk stamps and their four place names.
The lmlk system began after 732 BC, not only for 704–701 BC.

events.title: The siege of Lachish
events.text: Lachish, Judah's second city, was taken by Sennacherib in 701 BC. On the mound archaeologists found the Assyrian siege ramp, the defenders' counter-ramp, hundreds of arrowheads and a city burnt to the ground. At Nineveh, Sennacherib lined a room of his palace with carved panels of the siege, with the caption: 'Sennacherib, king of the world, king of Assyria, sat on his throne and the booty of Lachish passed before him.'
events.why: It is one of the few battles of the ancient world seen from both sides: in the ground at Lachish and on the walls of the conqueror's palace. The panels show the families of Lachish going into exile.
claims: Level III destroyed in 701 BC; the siege ramp and counter-ramp.
The Lachish room and its epigraph.

pic.cap: Assyrian archers attack Lachish: relief from Sennacherib's palace at Nineveh, British Museum. Photograph by Mike Peel (www.mikepeel.net), CC BY-SA 4.0.

events.title: Like a bird in a cage
events.text: Sennacherib says he took 46 walled cities of Judah and shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem 'like a bird in a cage', and that Hezekiah later sent 30 talents of gold, 800 of silver, his daughters and his singers after him to Nineveh. The Bible says Hezekiah paid 300 talents of silver and 30 of gold, but that the angel of the Lord struck the Assyrian camp, and Sennacherib went home.
events.why: Both agree that Jerusalem was not taken and that Hezekiah stayed on his throne. Why Sennacherib left is still debated: disease, news from elsewhere, or simply a deal that suited him. Herodotus heard an Egyptian version, in which mice ate the Assyrians' bowstrings.
claims: 46 cities, the bird in a cage, and the tribute sent to Nineveh: Sennacherib's annals.
The payment, the Rabshakeh, Isaiah and the angel: 2 Kings 18–19; Isaiah 36–37.

events.title: A smaller Judah
events.text: Sennacherib cut off the towns he had taken and gave them to Mitinti of Ashdod, Padi of Ekron and Silli-Bel of Gaza. In the lowlands many towns lay in ruins and were only partly rebuilt in the following decades. In 681 BC Sennacherib was murdered by his own son, as a Babylonian chronicle and the Bible both record.
events.why: Jerusalem had survived, and Jewish tradition remembered its rescue as a sign of God's care. The Talmud says God wished to make Hezekiah the Messiah. But Judah now lived as a small vassal of Assyria, in the hills around its capital.
claims: Judah's towns given to Ashdod, Ekron and Gaza.
Lowland towns destroyed in 701 BC and partly reoccupied under Manasseh.
Sennacherib killed by his son in 681 BC.
Killed by his sons in the house of his god: 2 Kings 19:37.

steps.text: Judah survived, but much smaller. Sennacherib says he cut off the towns he had taken, and gave them to the kings of Ashdod, Ekron and Gaza.
claims: Judah survived, but much smaller. Sennacherib says he cut off the towns he had taken, and gave them to the kings of Ashdod, Ekron and Gaza.

steps.text: Excavations show many towns of the lowlands destroyed in seven oh one, and only partly rebuilt in the decades that followed.
claims: Excavations show many towns of the lowlands destroyed in seven oh one, and only partly rebuilt in the decades that followed.
steps.display: Excavations show many towns of the lowlands destroyed in 701 BC, and only partly rebuilt in the decades that followed.

steps.text: Imagine the first morning after the army has gone, and the gates of Jerusalem opening again onto empty roads.

vignette.alt: Early morning, townspeople walking out of a city gate onto an empty road through quiet hills, old campfire rings by the road
vignette.caption: The gates open (impression)

steps.text: Twenty years later, in six eighty one BC, Sennacherib was killed by his own son. A Babylonian chronicle records it, and the Bible tells it too: he was struck down while he worshipped in the house of his god.
claims: Twenty years later, in 681 BC, Sennacherib was killed by his own son. A Babylonian chronicle records it.
He was struck down by his sons while he worshipped in the house of his god.
steps.display: Twenty years later, in 681 BC, Sennacherib was killed by his own son. A Babylonian chronicle records it, and the Bible tells it too: he was struck down while he worshipped in the house of his god.

steps.text: In Jewish memory, the rescue of Jerusalem became a sign of God's care for his city. The Talmud even says that God wished to make Hezekiah the Messiah.
claims: In Jewish memory, the rescue of Jerusalem became a sign of God's care for his city. The Talmud even says that God wished to make Hezekiah the Messiah.

steps.text: Jerusalem had been spared. But a little more than a century later, a new power, Babylon, will come to its gates. That is where our next chapter begins.
claims: A little more than a century later, Babylon will come to Jerusalem's gates.

vignette.alt: A walled hill city of stone houses at sunset, dark storm clouds gathering on the far horizon
vignette.caption: Jerusalem spared (impression)

steps.text: Chapter Six, in two minutes.
Hezekiah, son of Ahaz, becomes king of Judah. The Bible says he trusted in the Lord, the God of Israel, so that there was none like him among all the kings of Judah.
claims: Hezekiah, son of Ahaz, becomes king of Judah. The Bible says he trusted in the Lord, the God of Israel, so that there was none like him among all the kings of Judah.

steps.text: His son Sennacherib becomes king, and moves the capital to Nineveh. All over the empire, subject kings see their chance.
claims: His son Sennacherib becomes king, and moves the capital to Nineveh. All over the empire, subject kings see their chance.

vignette.alt: Huge city walls and gates beside a wide river with boats, palaces on a high mound behind
vignette.caption: Nineveh on the Tigris (impression)

steps.text: Under the City of David, a tunnel more than five hundred metres long carries the water of the Gihon spring to a pool inside the walls.
claims: Under the City of David, a tunnel more than five hundred metres long carries the water of the Gihon spring to a pool inside the walls.
steps.display: Under the City of David, a tunnel more than 500 metres long carries the water of the Gihon spring to a pool inside the walls.

vignette.alt: A narrow tunnel cut through rock, water running along the floor, lit by a small clay oil lamp
vignette.caption: Inside the tunnel (impression)

steps.text: In seven oh one BC, Sennacherib marches west.
claims: In seven oh one BC, Sennacherib marches west.
steps.display: In 701 BC, Sennacherib marches west.

steps.text: Then he turns on Judah. Forty six of Hezekiah's walled cities, he writes, and small towns without number, I besieged and conquered.
claims: Then he turns on Judah. Forty six of Hezekiah's walled cities, he writes, and small towns without number, I besieged and conquered.
steps.display: Then he turns on Judah. 46 of Hezekiah's walled cities, he writes, and small towns without number, I besieged and conquered.

steps.text: The greatest prize was Lachish, Judah's second city, guarding the road from the coast into the hills.
claims: The greatest prize was Lachish, Judah's second city, guarding the road from the coast into the hills.

steps.text: Now Jerusalem. Sennacherib writes: Hezekiah himself I shut up in Jerusalem, his royal city, like a bird in a cage.
claims: Now Jerusalem. Sennacherib writes: Hezekiah himself I shut up in Jerusalem, his royal city, like a bird in a cage.

vignette.alt: A walled city on a ridge at dusk, small army camps with fires on the hills around it, one bird flying above
vignette.caption: Like a bird in a cage (impression)

steps.text: Hezekiah tears his clothes and sends to the prophet Isaiah. Isaiah answers. He shall not come into this city, nor shoot an arrow there. For I will defend this city, to save it, for my own sake, and for my servant David's sake.
claims: Hezekiah tears his clothes and sends to the prophet Isaiah. Isaiah answers. He shall not come into this city, nor shoot an arrow there. For I will defend this city, to save it, for my own sake, and for my servant David's sake.

steps.text: The Bible tells what came next. That night the angel of the Lord went out, and struck down a hundred and eighty five thousand in the camp of Assyria. And Sennacherib went home, and stayed at Nineveh.
claims: The Bible tells what came next. That night the angel of the Lord went out, and struck down a hundred and eighty five thousand in the camp of Assyria. And Sennacherib went home, and stayed at Nineveh.
steps.display: The Bible tells what came next. That night the angel of the Lord went out, and struck down 185,000 in the camp of Assyria. And Sennacherib went home, and stayed at Nineveh.

vignette.alt: A silent army camp of tents among dark hills at night, fires burned down, a beam of light falling from the clouds
vignette.caption: That night (story)

steps.text: Sennacherib tells it differently. After I left, he says, Hezekiah sent his tribute after me to Nineveh. Thirty talents of gold, eight hundred talents of silver, ivory couches, his own daughters, and singers, men and women.
claims: Sennacherib tells it differently. After I left, he says, Hezekiah sent his tribute after me to Nineveh. Thirty talents of gold, eight hundred talents of silver, ivory couches, his own daughters, and singers, men and women.
steps.display: Sennacherib tells it differently. After I left, he says, Hezekiah sent his tribute after me to Nineveh. 30 talents of gold, 800 talents of silver, ivory couches, his own daughters, and singers, men and women.

steps.text: And Sennacherib never says that he took Jerusalem.
claims: And Sennacherib never says that he took Jerusalem.

steps.text: The story so far.
In twelve oh seven BC, an Egyptian victory stone names a people called Israel, in Canaan. It is the oldest known mention of the name.
claims: In twelve oh seven BC, an Egyptian victory stone names a people called Israel, in Canaan. It is the oldest known mention of the name.
steps.display: In 1207 BC, an Egyptian victory stone names a people called Israel, in Canaan. It is the oldest known mention of the name.

steps.text: Canaan is ruled by Egypt then, in a world of great empires.
claims: Canaan is ruled by Egypt then, in a world of great empires.

steps.text: Then the old world of the Bronze Age breaks down. Philistines settle on the coast, and small villages fill the hills.
claims: Then the old world of the Bronze Age breaks down. Philistines settle on the coast, and small villages fill the hills.

steps.text: Jewish tradition remembers this as the time of the Judges, and of the first kings.
claims: Jewish tradition remembers this as the time of the Judges, and of the first kings.

steps.text: The Bible tells of David and Solomon, ruling from Jerusalem, and of the temple Solomon built.
claims: The Bible tells of David and Solomon, ruling from Jerusalem, and of the temple Solomon built.

steps.text: How large their kingdom was is debated. But by about nine thirty BC there are two kingdoms: Israel in the north, and Judah in the south.
claims: How large their kingdom was is debated.
By about 930 BC there are two kingdoms: Israel in the north, and Judah in the south.
steps.display: How large their kingdom was is debated. But by about 930 BC there are two kingdoms: Israel in the north, and Judah in the south.

steps.text: Pharaoh Sheshonq, the Bible's Shishak, marches through the land, and lists the places he took on a temple wall at Karnak.
claims: Pharaoh Sheshonq, the Bible's Shishak, marches through the land, and lists the places he took on a temple wall at Karnak.

steps.text: Israel grows strong under Omri and Ahab, with its capital at Samaria. Then Assyria arrives, and King Jehu pays it tribute.
claims: Israel grows strong under Omri and Ahab, with its capital at Samaria. Then Assyria arrives, and King Jehu pays it tribute.

steps.text: Under Jeroboam the Second, Israel grows rich, and the prophets Amos and Hosea speak of justice and faithfulness.
claims: Under Jeroboam the Second, Israel grows rich.
The prophets Amos and Hosea speak of justice and faithfulness.

steps.text: Then Assyria returns to stay. Tiglath-pileser the Third takes Damascus and Galilee, and in seven twenty two BC Samaria falls.
claims: Then Assyria returns to stay. Tiglath-pileser the Third takes Damascus and Galilee, and in seven twenty two BC Samaria falls.
steps.display: Then Assyria returns to stay. Tiglath-pileser III takes Damascus and Galilee, and in 722 BC Samaria falls.

steps.text: Many of Israel's people are carried off to Assyria. In the south, Judah survives, as a vassal of the empire.
claims: Many of Israel's people are carried off to Assyria. In the south, Judah survives, as a vassal of the empire.
